questions.enonce_markdown:
Distinguish between the following transmission types:

(a) Synchronous and Asynchronous transmission. (2 marks)

(b) Broadband and Baseband transmission. (2 marks)

(c) Parallel and Serial transmission. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Synchronous and asynchronous transmission (2 marks)**

| Synchronous | Asynchronous |
|---|---|
| Data are sent as a **continuous stream of blocks (frames)**, the sender and the receiver being kept **in step by a common clock signal** (or clock bits in the data). | Data are sent **one character at a time**, with a **start bit and a stop bit** (and often a parity bit) around each character, so **no common clock** is needed. |
| No gaps between characters, so it is **fast and efficient** for large amounts of data (for example between computers or on a leased line). | The gaps and the extra start/stop bits make it **slower** and less efficient, but it is **simple and cheap** (keyboard, modem, serial mouse). |

**(b) Broadband and baseband transmission (2 marks)**

| Baseband | Broadband |
|---|---|
| The **whole bandwidth of the cable is used by one digital signal** at a time; only one channel. | The bandwidth is **divided into several channels (frequency multiplexing)**, so **several signals (data, voice, video) are carried at the same time**. |
| Short or medium distances, for example Ethernet on a LAN. | Longer distances and more capacity, for example cable television, ADSL and fibre links. |

**(c) Parallel and serial transmission (2 marks)**

| Parallel | Serial |
|---|---|
| **Several bits (for example 8 or 16) are sent at the same time**, each on its own wire. | The bits are sent **one after another along a single wire or channel**. |
| Fast over **short distances** (inside the computer, old printer port), but expensive cables and **skew/crosstalk** on long distances. | Slower per line but **reliable over long distances**, cheap cabling; used by USB, Ethernet, modems. |

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) State TWO benefits of normalisation in a database design. (2 marks)

(b) What is the role of Indexing data in a DBMS? (1 mark)

(c) Which category of relationships allows data to be linked from one table to several other tables in a relational database? (2 marks)

(d) A hospital keeps records of its patients. Give TWO rights of a patient on his personal data stored in this system. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Two benefits of normalisation (2 marks)**

- It **removes redundancy**: each fact is stored once, so the database is smaller.
- It **avoids update, insertion and deletion anomalies**, so the data stay **consistent and accurate** (integrity); the structure is also easier to maintain and extend. (Other acceptable point: queries are more flexible and efficient.)

**(b) Role of an index (1 mark)**

An index is a separate ordered list of the values of a field (key) with **pointers to the records**; it lets the DBMS **find, search and sort records quickly** without reading the whole table.

**(c) Category of relationship (2 marks)**

The **one-to-many (1:M) relationship**: one record of a table (for example one class or one customer) is linked to **several records** of another table (several students, several orders), through a **primary key and a foreign key**. (A many-to-many relationship is broken down into two one-to-many relationships by means of a link table.)

**(d) Two rights of a patient (2 marks)**

- The right to **access** his own records and to know what is held about him.
- The right to have **incorrect data corrected**.
- (Also acceptable: the right that the data are **kept confidential** and **not disclosed to a third party without consent**; that they are used **only for the purpose for which they were collected**; and that they are **not kept longer than necessary**.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain the mode of functioning of the following printers.

(a) Laser printer. (2 marks)

(b) Dot matrix printer. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Laser printer (2 marks)**

1. A **laser beam**, controlled by the page data, **draws the image on a rotating photosensitive drum** that has first been given an electrostatic charge; the parts hit by the light **lose their charge**.
2. **Toner** (a fine powder of plastic and pigment) is attracted to the discharged (or charged) image areas of the drum.
3. The paper is given a charge and passes against the drum: the **toner is transferred to the paper**.
4. The paper then goes through the **fuser** (hot rollers) which **melts the toner and presses it into the paper**. The drum is cleaned and discharged for the next page.

The whole page is built at once, which is why it is fast and quiet.

**(b) Dot matrix printer (2 marks)**

It is an **impact printer**. The **print head**, carrying a column of **9 or 24 fine pins**, moves **line by line across the paper**. For each character the control circuit fires the right pins; they **strike an inked ribbon against the paper** and leave a pattern of **dots** that forms the character. The paper is moved up by a tractor feed or a roller. Because of the impact it is **noisy** but can print **carbon copies** (multi-part stationery).
